findings.description: The new anthropic:claude-headless row records a static posture (execution_mode: remote_model; file_read/file_write/command_execution/network_access all false) for an adapter that spawns a local `claude -p` process in the operator's environment. The row's own notes concede that the posture only holds while the catalog's `extra.allowed_tools` stays empty. Nothing in test_trust_scopes.py ties this registry row to that adapter configuration, and `claude -p` also loads project-level settings from the cwd (hooks, .mcp.json servers) which `--tools ""` is not documented to exclude. In a P0 trust registry, a capability that is actually governed by a sibling config field is being asserted as a constant.
findings.failure_mode: A later sprint or an operator sets extra.allowed_tools on the claude-headless catalog entry, or the repo gains an MCP server config. The CLI hop now has real tool, file or network capability while the registry still says all-false and grants context_access.security: redacted on that basis. Every trust-scope test stays green because none of them read the adapter config.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a test alongside test_every_anthropic_catalog_entry_has_a_row that loads the catalog's claude-headless entry and asserts extra.allowed_tools is absent or empty (and, if the adapter supports it, that --strict-mcp-config is passed with no servers), with a failure message that points at this registry row. Alternatively give CLI-transport hops a distinct execution_mode (e.g. local_cli) so consumers can distinguish them from pure HTTP remotes rather than relying on prose in notes.

findings.description: This change adds eleven near-identical rows across two sections of a hand-maintained security registry. yaml.safe_load, used by _load_permissions and presumably by the runtime consumer, silently resolves duplicate mapping keys to the last occurrence. Neither the existing schema tests nor the two new tests detect duplicates, so a second definition of a key such as anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6 or anthropic:claude-opus-5-5 placed later in the file (a likely copy-paste outcome given the row shape) would shadow the intended row while test_current_generation_rows_mirror_the_4_7_scopes and test_every_anthropic_catalog_entry_has_a_row both keep passing against the surviving definition.
findings.failure_mode: Silent widening or narrowing of a model's trust scopes via a duplicate key in the registry, with CI green and no diagnostic.
findings.suggested_fix: In _load_permissions, load with a yaml.SafeLoader subclass whose construct_mapping raises on duplicate keys, and add a test that asserts the file loads under that loader. This is a few lines and closes the gap for every future row addition, not just this one.

findings.description: The mirror test pins only six of the eleven rows this diff adds. anthropic:claude-fable-5, anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6, anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929, anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 and anthropic:claude-headless each carry a note saying their scopes were copied from the 4.7 entry, but they are only checked for schema validity by the generic tests. findings.description: The new stderr capture creates a temp file with mktemp and removes it with a plain `rm -f` after the model-invoke call returns. There is no EXIT/INT/TERM trap. The adapter is routinely run under a caller-imposed timeout (flatline orchestrator, red-team pipeline, jury panel per-panelist timeout). When the caller kills the adapter mid-call, the `rm -f` never runs and the file, containing cheval's stderr, is left in TMPDIR. Separately, under `set -e` a failing mktemp (full or unwritable TMPDIR) now aborts the adapter before the model is invoked, a dependency the previous `2>/dev/null` path did not have.
findings.failure_mode: Orphaned `model-adapter-stderr.XXXXXX` files accumulate in /tmp across timed-out runs; on hosts with a read-only or full TMPDIR every model-adapter call fails before reaching cheval with only mktemp's message as diagnostics.
findings.suggested_fix: Register `trap 'rm -f -- "$err_file"' RETURN` (or EXIT in a subshell) right after mktemp, and fall back to `/dev/null` if mktemp fails: `err_file=$(mktemp ...) || err_file=/dev/null`. Alternatively avoid the file entirely with `2> >(grep -F -- 'gemini-headless dispatches agy' | cut -c1-600 >&2)`.

findings.description: cheval's stderr is now captured to a file, but only lines matching the agy WARN are forwarded. When `exit_code -ne 0` the script still reports only `model-invoke failed with exit code N` and deletes the file, so the actual provider/resolver error (unknown alias, auth failure, ceiling exceeded) is discarded even though it is already in hand. This matters more after this PR because six call sites now pass catalog aliases (`opus`, `cheap`, `reviewer`) whose resolution failures surface only on cheval's stderr.
findings.failure_mode: Operators debugging a failed Flatline/red-team/jury run see an opaque exit code and must re-run cheval by hand to learn that an alias did not resolve.
findings.suggested_fix: On non-zero exit, emit a bounded, control-stripped tail of `$err_file` to stderr (e.g. `tail -n 5 | cut -c1-600`) before removing it, or always when `LOA_DEBUG=true`.

findings.description: RES-4 uses bare negated commands as assertions: `! grep -q 'claude-opus-4-7' .../hitl-jury-panel/SKILL.md` and `! grep -q 'claude-3-5-sonnet' .../alternative-model.md`. Under bats-core, test bodies run with `set -eET` plus an ERR trap, and bash exempts `!`-inverted commands from both errexit and the ERR trap. Neither line is the final command of the test, so a non-zero result from `! grep` is simply discarded. This is the documented bats gotcha ("My negated statement does not fail the test"), which is why bats 1.5.0 added `run !`. The two residue checks therefore can never go red, even though RES-4 is cited as G-4 acceptance evidence for AC 1 (no previous-generation pins in hitl-jury-panel or the persona).
findings.failure_mode: If `claude-opus-4-7` is reintroduced into hitl-jury-panel/SKILL.md, or `claude-3-5-sonnet` into alternative-model.md, RES-4 still passes 7/7 and the residue gate reports clean. The 'red first' claim for this test cannot hold for these two assertions because they are unconditionally true.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `bats_require_minimum_version 1.5.0` to setup() and rewrite as `run ! grep -q 'claude-opus-4-7' "$R/.claude/skills/hitl-jury-panel/SKILL.md"` and `run ! grep -q 'claude-3-5-sonnet' "$R/.claude/data/personas/alternative-model.md"`. Alternatively use the pattern already used in RES-6: `run grep -q ...; [ "$status" -eq 1 ]`. Verify the fix goes red by temporarily inserting the forbidden string.

The implementation report says the entry is 'vendor-sourced' for input/output but does not mention cache read, and this test now locks the 5% figure in.

findings.suggested_fix: Re-check the cache_read_per_mtok value for claude-opus-5-5 against the vendor pricing page and the ratio used by the other Anthropic entries in model-config.yaml. If the vendor figure is $0.40, update both the catalog entry and the RES-1 expectation to 400000.

findings.failure_mode: If the hunk really lives in the persona file, a bats test body is injected into every alternative-model panelist prompt and RES-4/RES-6 greps over .claude/data will scan test fixtures as if they were persona text. If the path is mislabeled, the T5 expectation change (claude-sonnet-4-6 to claude-sonnet-5) was reviewed against the wrong file and its real location was not covered by this review.
findings.suggested_fix: Verify with `git show <commit> --stat` which file actually contains the T5 test. If it is the persona file, move the test to tests/unit and keep the persona document prose-only. If it is mislabeled, re-run the review bundle against the correct path.

findings.anchor: .claude/hooks/compliance/implement-gate.sh:Mode: heuristic unless the operator opts in through .loa.config.yaml
findings.description: The new authoritative-mode opt-in is read from `$PROJECT_ROOT/.loa.config.yaml`, but that file is inside the project workspace and is not protected by this hook because it is outside the App Zone. A model/session can first write `.loa.config.yaml` with `implement_gate.mode: authoritative`, then send a model-authored `tool_input.active_skill` such as `implement` and silently allow subsequent `src/`, `lib/`, or `app/` writes. This violates the stated invariant that only an operator opt-in selects authoritative mode and that model-authored `tool_input` must not select or bypass the gate.
findings.failure_mode: A forged two-step write bypasses the App Zone compliance ask: write project config to enable authoritative mode, then perform an App Zone Write/Edit with forged `tool_input.active_skill=implement`; the hook exits 0 without `decision: ask`.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not trust repo-local `.loa.config.yaml` for this security decision. Move the opt-in to an operator-controlled location outside the project writable surface, require an environment variable set by the harness/operator, or make writes to `.loa.config.yaml` that affect `implement_gate.mode` fail-ask/protected before the mode can change.

findings.description: The change moves the authoritative-mode trust anchor from .run/platform-features.json to $PROJECT_ROOT/.loa.config.yaml on the stated grounds that tool_input is model-authored and so nothing the model can write may select the mode. But .loa.config.yaml is also a plain file inside the project that the model writes with the same Write/Edit tools, and this very hook classifies it as non-App-Zone and exits 0 silently (zone check: only src/, lib/, app/ are gated). A model can therefore (1) Write .loa.config.yaml with `implement_gate:\n  mode: authoritative`, then (2) Write src/x.ts with tool_input.active_skill: "implement" and receive a silent allow with no ask and no audit line. IG-5 ("whatever .run/ claims") and IG-11 (key stays undocumented) pin a property that only holds if some other hook protects .loa.config.yaml; the hook source itself is readable to the model, so the undocumented key is not a control. The old code also logged compliance.mode.change to audit.jsonl; the new selection path writes nothing, so an authoritative session leaves no trace of why App Zone writes were allowed.
findings.failure_mode: If no separate hook guards .loa.config.yaml writes, the operator-only opt-in is self-grantable by the model in two tool calls, and every subsequent App Zone write with a forged active_skill bypasses the FAIL-ASK gate silently and unlogged.
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) have this hook treat writes to $PROJECT_ROOT/.loa.config.yaml (and .loa.config.yaml.* ) as gated, emitting {"decision":"ask"} regardless of zone, or confirm an existing protected-files hook covers it and reference it in the header comment; (b) read the opt-in from a location the model cannot author via tool_input (operator shell env var or ~/.config/loa/), falling back to the repo file only for display; and (c) restore an audit.jsonl event (e.g. compliance.mode.selected with source: .loa.config.yaml) whenever compliance_mode becomes authoritative, so an allowed write is attributable.

findings.description: Mode selection requires `command -v yq` and runs `yq '.implement_gate.mode // ""' file`. If yq is absent, or is Go yq v3 (which uses `yq r FILE PATH` syntax and errors on this expression), or is the Python jq-wrapper yq with a YAML the wrapper rejects, the error is swallowed by `2>/dev/null || configured_mode=""` and the operator's explicit opt-in is silently ignored. Nothing is written to audit.jsonl or stderr. The hook also calls yq on every App Zone write rather than once, so the silent failure repeats indefinitely. The quote-stripping `${configured_mode//\"/}` papers over the Python-vs-Go output difference but not the v3 syntax difference.
findings.failure_mode: An operator who sets implement_gate.mode: authoritative on a machine with yq v3 or no yq gets heuristic behaviour with no indication; because the fallback direction is toward asking, the symptom is spurious ADVISORY prompts that look like a hook bug rather than a missing dependency.
findings.suggested_fix: When .loa.config.yaml exists and contains the implement_gate key (cheap grep) but yq is missing or exits non-zero, append a one-line compliance.config.unreadable event to $RUN_DIR/audit.jsonl (guarded by the same once-only pattern used by the evidence recorder) and/or emit a single stderr note. Prefer the repository's existing config-reading helper if one exists so yq-flavour handling lives in one place.

findings.cross_file_justification: The new evidence recorder in implement-gate.sh creates or rewrites .run/platform-features.json via mktemp+mv, which refreshes the file's mtime. detect-platform-features.sh owns that file and, per the new test IG-9 (which must `touch -d '2 hours ago'` before invoking it), uses an mtime-based freshness cache.
findings.description: When no platform-features.json exists yet, the recorder writes a three-key object ({active_skill_available:false, active_skill_seen_at, active_skill_source}) with a brand-new mtime. If detect-platform-features.sh treats a file younger than its cache window as authoritative and returns it without re-detecting, every other feature field it normally populates (detected_at, schema_version, harness_signal, any further platform flags) is absent for the rest of the window, and any consumer reading those fields sees null. The same applies when the recorder rewrites an existing file: its mtime is bumped, extending the cache lifetime of possibly stale detections by up to the full window.
findings.failure_mode: For up to the cache window after the first lead-session payload carrying active_skill, `/loa` status and any other reader of platform-features.json may operate on a sparse or stale detection record because the file looks freshly detected.
findings.suggested_fix: Have the recorder preserve the original mtime (e.g. `touch -r "$FEATURES_FILE" "$_ig_tmp"` before mv when the file existed), or have detect-platform-features.sh key its cache on `.detected_at` rather than mtime and treat a file lacking detected_at as a cache miss. Add a bats case: recorder runs on an absent file, then detect runs within the window and still performs detection.

findings.description: CH-T8, CH-T9, IG-7, IG-8 and the opt-in half of IG-10 all `skip "yq not installed"`. The implementation report claims CH-T8 "no longer passes vacuously", but on any CI image without yq the entire authoritative branch of implement-gate.sh (the only branch that can produce a silent allow on a forged payload) runs zero assertions and the suite is green. The gate code itself also degrades silently without yq (DISS-002), so a missing yq hides both the behaviour and its tests at once.
findings.failure_mode: A regression in the authoritative branch (e.g. a widened case pattern or a dropped fallback) ships undetected on CI runners that lack yq, while local runs with yq pass; the report's non-vacuity claim does not hold in that environment.
findings.suggested_fix: Declare yq as a required test dependency and fail rather than skip when running under CI (e.g. `[[ -n "${CI:-}" ]] && fail "yq required" || skip`), or vendor a minimal yq-free parser path for the single scalar key so the branch is testable everywhere and the skip can be removed.

findings.description: rule_key returns 1 for anything that is not literally Bash(...), so the documented bare rule `Bash` ("matches all Bash commands") is silently dropped from both allow_by and deny_by. `Bash(*)` is likewise keyed as the exact rule `=*` and never matches. permissions.defaultMode (bypassPermissions / acceptEdits) is also not consulted. The header now claims the checker evaluates rules "the way Claude Code evaluates them" and the report says it "reads both rule grammars", but these forms remain unmodelled.
findings.failure_mode: A machine with `"allow": ["Bash"]` (common for autonomous setups) gets every one of the 16 requirements reported as missing and exit 1, blocking Run Mode preflight on a correctly permissioned machine. Conversely `"deny": ["Bash"]` or `"deny": ["Bash(*)"]` in any layer is ignored, the preflight passes, and the unattended run stalls on the first permission prompt, which is exactly the failure the preflight exists to prevent.
findings.suggested_fix: In rule_key, accept `Bash` and `Bash(*)` (after trim) and map them to a sentinel key such as `*` ; in main, treat deny_by['*'] as denying every requirement and allow_by['*'] as satisfying every requirement, in that order. Optionally read .permissions.defaultMode and short-circuit to PASS for bypassPermissions. Add CP cases for bare Bash in allow and in deny.

findings.description: The rewrite adds `command -v jq &>/dev/null || exit 0` and deletes the heredoc fallback, so on a host without jq .run/platform-features.json is never created or refreshed. Previously the file was always written (schema_version 1 via heredoc). Any consumer that distinguishes 'file absent' from 'harness_signal: false' now sees a different state on jq-less hosts, and a stale v1 file on such a host is never replaced.
findings.failure_mode: On a jq-less machine the probe becomes a no-op: no schema 2 file, no refresh of detected_at, and an existing schema 1 file with active_skill_available: true persists indefinitely.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep a printf-based fallback that writes the fixed schema 2 document (all evidence fields null) when jq is missing, or explicitly document that the file is only produced when jq is present and make consumers treat absence as 'no signal'.

findings.description: The one-hour mtime cache is honoured without checking the document's shape. An existing schema_version 1 file, including one that recorded active_skill_available: true via the now-removed CLAUDE_ACTIVE_SKILL_AVAILABLE env var or the .active-skill-probe path, is left in place and reported as current until it ages out. The script's stated contract is that it 'never reports active_skill_available: true on its own', but it will leave such a file untouched for up to an hour after upgrade.
findings.failure_mode: Immediately after upgrading, /loa or any consumer reading the file sees schema 1 content with active_skill_available: true for up to 60 minutes, contradicting the new truthful-reporting contract.
findings.suggested_fix: Bypass the cache when `jq -e '.schema_version == 2 and .active_skill_available == false'` fails on the existing file, so legacy or inconsistent documents are rewritten on the next run regardless of mtime.

findings.cross_file_justification: implement-gate.sh (per the report) writes active_skill_seen_at / active_skill_source into the same .run/platform-features.json 'once, atomically'. detect-platform-features.sh reads those fields into $base, then later mv's a fresh document over the file. Both writers are atomic individually but the detect script's read-then-replace is not serialised against the gate's write.
findings.description: detect-platform-features.sh performs an unlocked read-modify-write: `base=$(jq ... "$FEATURES_FILE")`, then jq -n ... > $tmp, then `mv -f $tmp $FEATURES_FILE`. If the gate's PreToolUse hook records evidence between the read and the mv (the gate fires on every Write/Edit and the detect script runs on SessionStart/status), the gate's just-recorded active_skill_seen_at and active_skill_source are overwritten with the stale nulls captured in $base.
findings.failure_mode: The gate's single evidence record is silently lost. If the gate's 'once' guard is keyed on something other than the presence of active_skill_seen_at in this file, the evidence is never re-recorded and /loa reports 'active_skill evidence: none' for the rest of the session.
findings.suggested_fix: Serialise with `flock` on $RUN_DIR/.platform-features.lock around read+write in both scripts, or have the detect script only ever update detected_at/schema fields via `jq ... "$FEATURES_FILE" > $tmp && mv` immediately after a fresh read (no separate $base capture), and have the gate re-record when it observes seen_at missing.

findings.cross_file_justification: The new --line branch reads .loa.config.yaml implement_gate.mode and labels the gate 'authoritative (opt-in; ...)', which confirms implement-gate.sh still accepts a config-selected authoritative mode. The report for this same sprint states the PreToolUse payload has no harness-set skill field and that tool_input.active_skill is model-forgeable; it says the mode is merely 'not documented' and that no .run file can select it.
findings.description: The --line output codifies an operator/config opt-in to a gate mode whose only input is a model-authored, forgeable field. If .loa.config.yaml is writable during a session (it is a project-root file, not under the framework-managed .claude/ zone), a model can set implement_gate.mode: authoritative and then supply tool_input.active_skill on each Write/Edit, bypassing the C-PROC-001 implement gate. Separately, when yq is absent the line prints 'heuristic' regardless of the configured mode, so the status line can misreport a security-relevant setting.
findings.failure_mode: Implement gate becomes bypassable by a two-step model-authored edit, and /loa may display 'heuristic' while the gate is actually running in authoritative mode.
findings.suggested_fix: Until a harness-set signal exists, have implement-gate.sh refuse or downgrade implement_gate.mode: authoritative (log a WARN and run heuristic), and extend the forged-payload bats case to assert that the config cannot select it. In --line, drop the 'opt-in' label or print an explicit WARN when authoritative is configured, and resolve the mode with the same parser/fallback the gate uses so the two never disagree.

findings.description: The diff records validate-skill-capabilities.sh as modified (index 13f633c6..0b7f30f3) but contains no hunk for it, and the P0 full-file context omits it. The YAML loader that now populates WRITE_CAPABLE_AGENTS, its 'general-purpose only' fallback, and its handling of a missing yq therefore cannot be reviewed. Note that the header comment of agent-types.yaml contains the literal token `write_capable: true` (line 4); a grep/awk-based loader that scans for that token and takes the preceding line as the agent name would ingest comment text.
findings.failure_mode: Unreviewable change to the P0 lint that enforces the #553 invariant. If the loader is text-based rather than a YAML parse, comment lines or future comments can pollute or widen the write-capable allowlist without reviewer visibility.
findings.suggested_fix: Resubmit the hunk. Ensure the loader parses YAML (e.g. `yq '.agent_types | to_entries[] | select(.value.write_capable == true) | .key'`) and falls back to `general-purpose` when yq is missing or the file fails to parse. Add bats cases for: file missing, yq missing, malformed YAML, a comment containing `write_capable: true`, and `claude`/`fork` accepted.

findings.description: `claude` and `fork` are registered as harness agent types with Write/Edit. Claude Code's documented SKILL.md `agent:` values are the built-in subagent types (general-purpose, Explore, Plan) or names of .claude/agents/*.md; `fork` is the value of the separate `context:` key, not an agent type, and `claude` is not a documented subagent_type. The rules doc now tells authors they may set `agent: fork` or `agent: claude` for file-authoring skills.
findings.failure_mode: A write-capable skill that sets `agent: fork` or `agent: claude` passes the lint, but its runtime dispatch depends on how the harness treats an unknown subagent type (error, or silent fallback), reintroducing the class of silent misdispatch #553 was meant to catch.
findings.suggested_fix: Verify both names against the Agent tool's subagent_type list in the target Claude Code version and record the provenance in the YAML comment; if they are not real types, remove them and keep the skill-invariants.md allowed list to general-purpose plus named .claude/agents entries.

findings.description: The new WRITE_CAPABLE_AGENTS loader falls back to ("general-purpose") whenever the array is empty, without distinguishing why it is empty. The header comment and SC-T-AGENT-9 describe the fallback as applying to 'a missing or unparsable file', but a present, well-formed agent-types.yaml in which every entry is write_capable: false (or in which .agent_types has no entries) also triggers it, silently re-enabling general-purpose for write-capable skills. The same branch swallows a missing `yq` binary or a yq syntax incompatibility (2>/dev/null || true) with no diagnostic, so the only visible symptom is the validator rejecting every `agent: claude` / `agent: fork` write skill with an error that lists only '(general-purpose)'. Note: the diff attributes this hunk to a `new file` header for .claude/data/agent-types.yaml, but the content is the validator script; the real path was not in the diff, so the anchor is by hunk header.
findings.failure_mode: An operator who edits agent-types.yaml to mark general-purpose write_capable: false with no other true entries expects general-purpose to be rejected, but the validator accepts it. Separately, on a CI host without yq (or with the Python yq wrapper, where `yq eval` fails), skills that legitimately set agent: claude or agent: fork fail validation with a misleading message and no indication that the data file was never read.
findings.suggested_fix: Capture yq's exit status separately from the result: run yq into a variable, fall back to general-purpose only when the file is absent or yq exited non-zero, and honour an empty parsed set as 'no agent may be named'. Emit a one-line stderr warning when the fallback is taken (e.g. 'agent-types.yaml unreadable; using built-in default general-purpose') so the misconfiguration is visible in CI logs. Add a test for the all-false file case to pin whichever semantics are intended.

findings.description: agent-types.yaml is now the single source of truth for which agent types have Write/Edit, but nothing verifies that its write_capable flags agree with the agent definitions they describe. SC-T-AGENT-7 asserts that every .claude/agents/*.md has a row and pins the exact current key/value string, but it does not read each agent's `tools:` frontmatter and compare. The invariant behind Issue #553 is precisely that a skill declaring write capability must not be bound to an agent whose allowlist lacks Write/Edit; with the flag now a hand-maintained boolean, a one-line edit to either file can desynchronise them and the test suite stays green.
findings.failure_mode: A future change marks a project agent write_capable: true in the YAML (or adds Write to an agent's tools without updating the YAML, or vice versa). In the fail-open direction, a skill with write_files: true and agent: <that type> passes validate-skill-capabilities.sh, then fails silently at runtime because the agent cannot call Write/Edit, which is the exact #553 symptom this mechanism exists to prevent. The hard-coded exact-string assertion also means every new agent file requires an unrelated test edit, encouraging reviewers to update the string reflexively rather than check the flag.
findings.suggested_fix: In SC-T-AGENT-7 (or a new SC-T-AGENT-10), for each .claude/agents/*.md parse the frontmatter `tools:` list and assert that `write_capable` equals whether Write or Edit appears in it; keep the harness-only types (general-purpose, claude, fork, Plan, Explore) as the explicitly enumerated exceptions. Replace the brittle exact-string equality with per-key assertions so adding an agent file only requires the derived check to pass.

findings.anchor: tests/unit/hook-guard.bats:parse-failure WARN does not call every wrapped hook a PreToolUse hook
findings.description: The new test (d) pins the WARN text with a bare `! grep -q "PreToolUse hook" "$err"` as a non-final line. Under bats' errexit/ERR-trap harness, a `!`-negated pipeline never triggers errexit (POSIX exempts it), and only the last command's status is used as the function's return. So the one assertion that is the stated purpose of this test cannot fail: if the hook-guard WARN regresses to say "PreToolUse hook" again, the test still passes because the following two positive greps succeed. The sibling tests CMP-277/CMP-278 in this same diff use the correct `[ -z "$(grep …)" ]` form.
findings.failure_mode: A future edit that reintroduces the misleading 'PreToolUse hook' wording in hook-guard.sh passes CI; the test provides no regression protection for the behaviour it claims to cover.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `run ! grep -q "PreToolUse hook" "$err"` (bats ≥1.5) or `! grep -q "PreToolUse hook" "$err" || false`, or mirror CMP-277's `[ -z "$(grep 'PreToolUse hook' "$err")" ]`.

findings.description: The freshness guard now trips every 12 hours (grace fixture's offline_valid_until) instead of every 30 days, and it compares `epoch > now` with zero margin. Two consequences: (1) a fixture with seconds left passes the guard in setup() but is already expired when the validator under test reads it a moment later, producing an unreproducible one-off failure; (2) regeneration is now a routine event rather than a once-per-checkout one, and the generator path (`cd $_ELF_DIR && python3 $_ELF_GEN`) has no lock and writes the pubkey and six signed JSONs non-atomically. Under `bats --jobs N`, two setup() calls that both observe a stale window run the generator concurrently; one test can copy a pubkey from one keypair alongside a license signed by the other, and every signature-dependent test in that file fails with an error that disappears on rerun. The race pre-existed for first generation, but the diff makes the trigger frequent.
findings.failure_mode: Intermittent, non-reproducible signature/grace failures in test_license_validator-style suites during parallel runs or at the 12-hour boundary; the ensure script is sourced from several bats files' setup() so the blast radius is every license test.
findings.suggested_fix: Require a safety margin (e.g. `epoch - now > 3600`) so a fixture that will expire during the run is regenerated up front; serialise regeneration with an `mkdir`-based lock (or `flock` where available) around the generator call and re-check freshness after acquiring it, so concurrent setups do not both regenerate.

findings.description: The bare-citation branch of CITE accepts any `:N` whose preceding character is not in `[A-Za-z0-9_./:]`. That admits quotes, brackets, braces and asterisks, so compact JSON/YAML/code in the review body becomes a line citation bound to the last cited path: `"critical":0`, `"high":2`, `{"line":40}`, `]:7`. The review's own `<!-- LOA-VERDICT {"counts":{"critical":0,"high":1,...}} -->` trailer, when emitted compactly (which is what json.dumps-with-separators or a template typically produces), adds one bare citation per count value to whichever file was cited last. The header contract added in this diff says a `:N` that is not a citation "credits nothing"; the regex does not implement that for non-word punctuation.
findings.failure_mode: After any path citation, the trailer's count values are credited as lines 0..k on that file. A defect anchored within ±3 of those values (lines 1–8 of the last-cited file: shebang, `set -euo pipefail`, import/header guard defects) is marked detected without being mentioned, inflating recall on the A/B gate this grader decides. `details.citations` is wrong on every review that has a trailer. RG-11..14 pass only because the fixture anchors sit at 7 and 40 and the helper's trailer counts are small; a `"high":4..10` or a `"critical":N` colliding with a low anchor flips the result.
findings.suggested_fix: Tighten the bare branch so the colon must be preceded by whitespace, start-of-text, `(`, `[` or a backtick, e.g. replace `(?<![A-Za-z0-9_./:])` with `(?<![^\s(\[`])` (fixed-width negated-class lookbehind; succeeds at position 0). Additionally strip the `<!-- LOA-VERDICT ... -->` trailer from `text` before running CITE.finditer, since it is parsed separately anyway. Add a bats case: `c.sh:100 is odd` followed by `{"counts":{"critical":7}}` must detect nothing.

findings.description: When a path is wrapped in inline code or bold and the line follows the closing delimiter (`` `b.sh`:40 ``, `**b.sh**:40`, `(b.sh):40`), alternative 1 fails because the delimiter sits between the extension and the colon, and alternative 2 then binds `:40` to the previously cited file. Under 1.0.0 these forms yielded no citation; under 1.1.0 they credit the wrong file. Separately, alternative 1 matches non-file tokens such as `example.com:8080` or `v1.2.3:40` (anything with a dot-suffix before a colon) and overwrites `last`, so later bare `:N` references bind to a URL host instead of the real prior file.
findings.failure_mode: A review that writes `a.sh:1 ... `c.sh`:7` is scored as citing a.sh:7 (possible spurious hit on a.sh, guaranteed miss on c.sh). A URL between a citation and a bare `:N` silently drops the bare reference. Both are deterministic scoring errors in the A/B measure, in opposite directions.
findings.suggested_fix: In alternative 1 allow optional closing delimiters between path and colon: `(?P<path>...)[`*)]{0,3}:`. For `last`, only update it when `path_matches` succeeds against at least one manifest file, or skip tokens whose extension is not a plausible source extension (e.g. reject when the path contains `//` or the ext is all digits).

findings.description: The comma continuation `(?:\s*,\s*RNG)*` in the `first` group has no boundary check after the number and `\s*` spans newlines, so any number that follows a citation and a comma is credited as another line on that path: `a.sh:40, 3 other sites`, `fixed in b.py:10, 2 commits ago`, `a.sh:40,\n2. Next finding`. With RNG's range syntax, `b.py:10, 2026-10-06` yields the range 10–2026 on b.py, which covers every defect in the file.
findings.failure_mode: Spurious line citations and, in the date case, a whole-file range that detects every planted defect in that file regardless of what the review said. The grader's stated rule is a ±3 window around a cited line; a swallowed prose number or date defeats it.
findings.suggested_fix: Require each continued number to be followed by a boundary that is not a word, hyphen or digit continuation, e.g. append `(?![A-Za-z0-9-])` after each RNG in the comma list, restrict the separator to `[ \t]*,[ \t]*` (no newlines), and cap ranges to a sane width (e.g. ignore a range wider than 200 lines or treat it as its first line only).

findings.description: The grader runs `python3 - ... <<'PY'` and imports `json` and `re`. With a stdin script, `sys.path[0]` is the current directory, and neither module is frozen, so a `json.py` or `re.py` in whatever directory the harness runs the grader from is imported in place of the stdlib. The grader reads an agent-produced review inside `$workspace`; if the eval harness invokes the grader with cwd set to that workspace (not ruled out by the script, which takes the workspace as an argument), the agent under evaluation can plant a module that prints a passing verdict. Pre-existing in 1.0.0, but this diff is the parser rewrite and the right moment to close it.
findings.failure_mode: Eval-integrity bypass: an agent writes `json.py` next to review.md, the grader executes it, and the recall gate reports pass/score=100 for any review. Also a correctness hazard if an unrelated `re.py` happens to exist in cwd.
findings.suggested_fix: Invoke as `python3 -I - "$manifest" "$review" "$executor" <<'PY'` (isolated mode: no cwd on sys.path, no user site, ignores PYTHON* env). Optionally `cd "$SCRIPT_DIR"` before the call.

findings.description: `sites = d.get("anchors") or [d["anchor_line"]]` ignores `anchor_line` entirely when `anchors[]` is non-empty and performs no type check. A manifest whose `anchors` omits `anchor_line` silently narrows detection; one with a string or null element raises TypeError inside the heredoc, so the grader prints a Python traceback with no JSON and exits 1, which the harness cannot distinguish from a legitimate recall failure. The documented contract is exit 2 with a JSON error for a bad manifest, and the only guard is RG-16, which checks the two committed manifests rather than the grader.
findings.failure_mode: A hand-edited or future manifest with a typo in `anchors` either under-counts detections without any signal, or crashes the grader into a non-JSON, exit-1 state that the A/B pipeline records as a failed review.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute `sites = {d["anchor_line"]} | set(d.get("anchors") or [])`, validate every site is an int (`isinstance(s, int) and not isinstance(s, bool)`), and on violation emit the standard error JSON and `sys.exit(2)` so the bash `err` contract holds.

findings.cross_file_justification: The diff changes the Agent Teams constraint rationales in the source constraints file, but the managed generated CLAUDE.loa.md block still contains the old rationale text and unchanged generated hash.
findings.description: The managed Loa instruction file is stale relative to .claude/data/constraints.json for the Agent Teams constraints. The source now says, for example, that planning skills produce single artifacts with single-writer semantics, but CLAUDE.loa.md still says only 'Planning skills assume single-writer semantics'. The generated block hash is also unchanged, indicating this section was not regenerated.
findings.failure_mode: Consumers that read CLAUDE.loa.md receive outdated generated policy text despite the source constraints changing. This violates the managed-file generation contract and can cause policy drift between the canonical constraints and the runtime instructions agents actually load.

findings.description: KF-040 records an Anthropic 400 'not allowed from unsupported countries, regions, or territories' and gives the standing workaround as routing the hop through Bedrock. The reading guide does say to check egress first, but the 'Current workaround' field, which is what a hurried operator and the ledger lint read, presents the route-around as the remedy. The 400 is a policy refusal, not a transport fault; if the host's egress genuinely terminates in an unsupported region, routing the same request through Bedrock is a terms-of-access bypass rather than an environmental fix.
findings.failure_mode: The ledger institutionalises 'use claude-bedrock' as the fix for a compliance refusal. Future recurrences get resolved by swapping routes with no record that the egress region was ever confirmed as permitted.
findings.suggested_fix: Reword 'Current workaround' to: confirm the host's egress region is permitted (VPN exit, cloud region); only then route through claude-bedrock for the run. Keep the Bedrock route in the Attempts row as what happened, not as the standing remedy.
